THOUGHT: The patient is a 65-year-old female with chronic sun exposure (reports sunbathing and outdoor walking), which is the primary risk factor for actinic keratosis (AK). The lesion is located on the dorsal hand—a classic sun-exposed site—and presents as a rough, scaly, sandpaper-like plaque without inflammation, pain, or tenderness—consistent with the clinical appearance of AK. Her age, fair-skin likelihood (inferred from sun sensitivity implied by sunbathing and development of photodamage), and absence of immunosuppression or other confounding dermatoses further support this. The skin biopsy is definitive: hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis reflect abnormal keratinocyte differentiation; solar elastosis confirms chronic UV damage; and atypical keratinocytes confined to the epidermis (i.e., no invasion into the dermis) are the histopathologic hallmark of actinic keratosis—representing a clonal proliferation of dysplastic keratinocytes and recognized as a precancerous lesion (SCC in situ if more extensive, but here limited to epidermis and consistent with AK). No features of squamous cell carcinoma (e.g., dermal invasion), basal cell carcinoma (e.g., palisading nuclei, stromal retraction), psoriasis (e.g., regular acanthosis, Munro microabscesses), or seborrheic keratosis (e.g., “stuck-on” appearance, horn cysts, no solar elastosis) are present.

DIAGNOSIS: Actinic keratosis
